Nanking Now. 8, 1937
Section 4
Dear Family:
Today was bright a d clear - not a cloud in the sky. The Japs
bombed a passenger train north of here killing two hundred innocent non-
corb attants
but they didn't bomb Nanking for which no doubt we have the
Brussels onference to thank. Mr. Peck and I had dinner with some old friends
Mr. and Mrs. Pan of the Ministry of Railways. It was interesting to hear first
hand of the marvelous job the railroads are doing - they keep the trains moving
under almost impossible odds.
In one instance over 1000 bombs of various sizes
were dropped on one short stretch of track but within twelve hours trains were
again operating over that stretch of roadbed.
The repair crews work at night
and sleep in dugouts during the day time. At Soochow they had an average of
eight hours of bombing for ten consecutive days but still kept the trains mor-
ing. If that sort of morale can pervade all services the Japs are going to
have a long and tough job ahead.
Nov. 9th. Beautiful day - no bomb raids. Chinese are asking bids
on 60 basic trainer airplanes - they must think the war will last a long time.
The Board meeting was postponed until tgmorrow - d--n it. I had planned to
leave tomorrow.
Bond can't get back to Nanking by car because all roads are
blocked.
He wired that he was coming by British boat and driving by car around
the boom in the Yangtze. He expeots to arrive here on Friday or Saturday. W11
probably wait until he comes as the boat I was planning to take leaves tomorrow
morning and there probably will not be another until the one he comes on.
ELELS
Someone - probably a peint salesmen - sold the Chinese on the idea of
painting all their buildings a dirty gray color - supposedly so they will not
be so conspicuous from the air. Of course all the bombing is done from great
heights and about the only thing the bomber can see is roofs - but nearly every
building is covered with that awful looking stuff - even statues, Ming Tomb
animels and the Sun Yat Sen Memorial. Don't know why the Japs overlooked that
Memorial and the Ming Tombs but though outside the wall neither of those "mil-
itary objectives" have been bombed. I predict they will be and when a howl is
raised the Japs will say that anti
Of course the Chhese
have been very careful not to give the Japanese any valid reason for bombing the
tomb of their George Washington.
Dined tonight with some of the American teachers at Nanking University
and some missionaries.
It was easy to tell which were which - most of the teach-
ers took a cocktail and smoked. The missionaries may do both - like a debutante
raiding the icebox - when they get home - but with the Ambassador and Mr. Peck
both present they were on their best behavior and wore the proper funerial grav-
ity which is the mode among missioneries when there is laughter or anyone is hav-
ing a good time.
Wed. Now. 10th. As I write this I am waiting for a meeting of the Board
of Directors of CNAC - the meeting was called for 3 o'clock but on arriving punc-
tually I am told in true very polite Chinese fashion that the meeting will not
be held until 4.
Of course they didn't think to call me up. At noon we had an
air raid - the first alarm came at 12:20 - a long siren followed by the beating
on brass gongs around town at strategic points so even the soundly sleeping
chauffeurs of waiting motor cars are awakened. The ceiling was about six thou-
sand feet and above that a solid overcast.
Three Jap planes came in from the
east, flew directly over the city in a V formation. They flew directly over the
American Embassy and released their bombs soon after crossing over.
Their target
was the military air fields from which all airplanes have long since departed, the
hangars are already a shambles and coolies repair the field as fast as the Japs
The Japs drop
tons of bombs, costing thousands of dollars, and report the destruction of say
ten enemy planes. That night the Chinese kite makers rebuild their paper planes,
move them to new positions and the next day the process is repeated. In this

manner the Japanese have reported the destruction of more airplanes than the
Chinese ever owned. I suppose the Japanese Foreign office will soon start
issuing claims of "non-cooperation" and "insincerity" and threaten to
measures."
As the planes went over the city the anti-aireraft guns out loose from
every side and machine guns rattled like the sound of driving rivets.
aircraft shells made black puffs of smoke in the gray sky around the plenes but
none exploded near enough to do any damage and the planes held their formation
and their course seemingly undisturbed by the noisy chorus from below.
bombs were dropped inside the wall which encircles the city.
Here in this room all lights are out and there is no heat. I am writ-
ing next to a window, one of two such openings with a door between, a small
amount of light filters in from the courtyard over the double row of sand bags
piled ceiling high in front of the door
and windows.
The room is one set aside
for meetings and o nferences.
It is on the first floor of the four storied mag-
nificent Ministry of Communications building built in modern steel and concrete
to resemble the old Chinese architecture.
am told that the floor above us is
covered with a double layer of sand bags
this room is considered reasonably
bomb-proof. I hope that statement is true
for the siren outside is at this
moment screaming the signal which warns
that another raid is on the way.
posts with telephone connections to the siren stations are flung around Nanking
in e circle so that warnings are given about 15 minutes before the planes get
here. To augment the siren a small boy walked through the corridor with
alarm clock ringing vociferously the while he wound it vigorously. Literally
We had our board meeting in the candle light - all lights
are off during raids - and I'll onfess that it was a bit eerie and disconcert-
ing until we got the
"all clear" signal, lights were
turned on and it was again
a case of business as usual. The Ministry building is checked an as an objective
on all the Jap maps
which have been taken from planes shot down.
Our meeting
was a total loss so far as getting anything accomplished along lines desired by us.
Had dinner at the Metropolitan Hotel with some of my American aviation
friens, all of whom are here trying
get "their share"
in each case
a11) of an order for seven million U. S. dollars worth of airplanes, motors
and parts.
They are all worried about deliveries and their schemes are legion
for beating the Japanese blockade and various American restrictive export regu-

Thur. Nov. 11th. Armistice Day - only in history•
This noon the siren
the same time as yesterday and 15 minutes later the drone of many
motors was audible but no planes in sight. Mr. Johnson, Mr. Peck and I left
the tiffin table and repaired to a little open porch near the roof. Next to
Mr. Peck's house, in which I am staying, is a large Chinese grave yard with lots
of mounds which provide good shelter against flying shrapnel.
The nearby Chinese
farmers, ricksha coolies and servants all congregate there when an alarm sounds.
there for the cover afforded by the hundreds of grave mounds and also
to be near the American flag which they at least think affords them some measure
of protection. The noise of the motors became louder and presently out of the
clouds to the south three Japanese twin-motored bombers came into view - below
the clouds at about 6000 feet.
The sky was about 95 percent overcast at that
altitude and only infrequent holes showed a light blue against the gray which
of course predominated.
The three bombers came directly at us then turned away
toward the airport outside the wall, where no doubt more paper planes had been

CAN CHINA SURVIVE by Hallet Abend and A. J. Billingham.
Translation of statement made by General Li Tsung-jen of Kwangsi in the early
summer of 1936.
"China's most urgent need today is the salvation of her people. In order
the Chinese people may attain liberty and equality with other peoples, and
lest China's territorial integrity be further jeopardized, the present impossible
state of affairs cannot be allowed to continue.
"We must be aroused from our lethargy. We must move our people to a strug-
gle for national emancipation. We must be
to answer our aggressors
with resolute measures and,
true to our great tradition of self-help and in-
dependence, to see our country reduced to ashes rather than submit. Only thus
In this way alone can we arrive at an anicable and permanent
solution of the Sino-Japanese problem.
"If we have
the determination to resist, the superiority of the Japanese
armed forces will meet with insurmountable
difficulties when confronted with
what seem to most people weakness'.
Militarily speaking, Japan's modern and
superior war mam ine will not know how to operate in a wide terrain with in-
numerabb people,
poor communications, and sources of supplies as yet un-
developed.
Under the same topographieal conditions our enemy can be brought
through exhaustion to eventual defeat if we, determined and united
adopt the
strategy of ever widening the area of hostilities and entangling the enemy on
all sides with the help of armed volunteers.
"Such strategy, if persisted in, will be fatal to Japan's existence as a
state, particularly when she is now practically alone in the world and has many
insoluble contradictions within her social and economic system.
Just as France
under lapoleon and Germany under William II, Japan,
though possibly victorious
in the beginning will be finally laid low, as befits all aggressors and all
users of brutal force.
"Economically speaking, China has the advantage of having no economic
and industrial centers as against the disadvantage of economic backwardness
primitive production.
If war comes Japan will of course blockade our seaports
and devastate our seacoasts, but those ports on our coast are mere centers of
trade and not centers of production so
that their destruction does not mean the
strangulation of our economie life.
"Our farmers will still be able to work and produce and give us self-
sufficiency.
With the low standard of living of our people and soldiers, their
patience, and their capacity for work and endurance,
they will be able to hold
on despite vast sacrifices.
"In contrast to China, Japan is a capitalist country with highly devel-
oped production.
The depression has aggravated her economic crisis and embit-
tered the already hard lot of her toiling masses. Her budget deficits have ex-
ceeded 800,000,000 yen, and her national debts increased to over 10,000,000,000
yen. Her manufacturers are being barred from the markets of the world.
lacks power resources, provisions, clothing materials, and other necessities.
A protracted war with
Japan will not only increase her military expensitures
to the point of unbearability, but will further improverish her proletariat,
and aggravate the economic crisis that now stalks in her political arena.
EHOLISIPIOS
